summary: A report on Utah's experiments measuring host costs for sending network data. Utah had run compute-bound jobs on its PDP-10 and moved them to UCLA's batch machine. The note gives the background and examples of the jobs, and then the timing work.

plainLanguage.summary: This report measures how much TENEX CPU time Utah spent transferring data to and from UCLA. The authors conclude that host processing and protocol work contributed substantially to the cost they measured.

questions: host costs of network data transmission
what did utah measure in rfc 392
how much cpu time did network transfer use

subtitle: Utah measures the TENEX CPU effort involved in transferring data over the network.

tldr.problem: Utah wanted to measure the host cost of sending jobs and data to UCLA's RJS, not the network's transmission rate.
tldr.mechanism: The authors timed the NETRJS program and calculated real time, chargeable CPU time and CPU microseconds per bit for transfers.
tldr.outcome: They report 75 to 85 microseconds of chargeable CPU time per bit and suggest changes to host software and protocols to reduce the cost.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 392 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The results describe one host program and its measured workload.

sections.title: Why Utah Measured Transfer Costs
sections.content:
Utah ran large compute-bound jobs, including algebraic simplification, differential-equation work and waveform processing. It developed a program to submit jobs to UCLA's Remote Job Service on an IBM 360/91.

The RJS protocol required transmitted data to be blocked, so the Utah program added record and block headers. The authors report that this computation and memory use contributed to page faulting and led them to rewrite the send and receive parts of the program.
sections.plainLanguage: Utah sent jobs to UCLA's batch computer. Preparing data in the form required by the service used memory and CPU time on the Utah host.

sections.title: How the Measurements Were Made
sections.content:
TENEX accessed the network as a file device using byte-in and byte-out operations. In fast mode, those operations took 120 microseconds per byte according to the report. A slower operation occurred once per message; with 36-bit bytes it averaged 500 microseconds and could take up to a millisecond when bytes had to be unpacked.

The authors timed file-to-network and network-to-file portions of the program. They emphasize that they were measuring the host cost of transfer, not network transmission rates. Their results showed 75 to 85 microseconds of chargeable CPU time per bit.
sections.plainLanguage: The team measured how much CPU time its program used while reading and writing network data. It did not attempt to measure the network's raw transmission speed.

sections.title: Estimated Cost and Possible Changes
sections.content:
Using a TENEX charge rate of $474.60 per CPU hour, the authors estimate that one million bits would cost $9.90 to $11.20 in CPU time at the sending host, and potentially a similar amount at the receiving host. They compare this with predicted network transmission costs and say the host cost was much higher.

Suggested changes include treating the network as an interprocess communication device rather than a file device, building an intelligent network input/output device, and allowing 32-bit bytes in the RJS-UCLA protocol instead of requiring 8-bit bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The report estimates that host CPU costs for a transfer could exceed the network transmission cost. It suggests improvements to host software and protocols rather than only to communication devices.

references.text: RFC 325, describing the Network Remote Job Entry Program NETRJS.
